name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,171

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Downright victory for a noted native son

blocks.note: a bald statement is a downright, blunt one
a win is a victory

explanation.surface: An outright win for some celebrated local boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noted native son' plays on Notes of a Native Son, the 1955 essay collection by James Baldwin.
explanation.definitionFit: The American writer James Baldwin published Notes of a Native Son, so the phrase is a playful allusion identifying him.

clue.text: Chemical protective covering around wheels

indicators.note: something placed around another surrounds it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: a bib protects clothes while eating
wheels is slang for a car

explanation.surface: A chemical coating applied round a vehicle's wheels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wheels' looks literal but is slang for a car; the bib goes around it.
explanation.definitionFit: Bicarb is short for bicarbonate of soda, a common household chemical compound.

clue.text: Lily’s a bit nimble

blocks.note: lis is the heraldic lily, as in fleur-de-lis
some is a bit of something

explanation.surface: Someone called Lily is rather agile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lily' reads as a girl's name, but it is the flower, LIS in heraldry and in fleur-de-lis.
explanation.definitionFit: Lissome describes a supple, graceful, agile body, which is a close synonym for nimble.

clue.text: The children’s book, originally about Peter and Mary, from America

definitions.text: The children’s book, originally about Peter and Mary, from America

blocks.note: surface reading: some book written for young readers

blocks.clueFragment: originally about Peter and Mary, from America
blocks.note: setter's reading: a novel first published as The Children, whose heroes are two American siblings lost in the Australian outback

explanation.surface: A description of a children's story about two American kids named Peter and Mary.
explanation.walkthrough: James Vance Marshall's 1959 novel was first titled The Children, so 'The Children's book' is that book, later renamed and filmed by Nicolas Roeg.
explanation.definitionFit: The novel is known today by its later title, which names the Aboriginal boy's ritual journey through the bush.

clue.text: See 21
Just a bit of a sequel?

definitions.text: Just a bit of a sequel?

blocks.note: surface reading: only a small part of something
setter's reading: 'just' is fair, and a sequel is a second, the Spanish for two

explanation.surface: Asking whether something is merely a fragment of a follow-up film or book.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags whimsy: 'Just' becomes an adjective for fairness and the sequel becomes a part two, in Spanish.
explanation.definitionFit: The British colloquial phrase means fair shares or just treatment, an informal plea for even-handed dealing.

clue.text: I could be small but as an actor I’m not

definitions.text: I could be small but as an actor I’m not

blocks.note: small young fish, and insignificant people, are called small by this name

blocks.clueFragment: but as an actor I’m not
blocks.note: the British actor Stephen of this surname is famously tall

explanation.surface: A riddle in which the speaker is little in one role but not on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small fry' means minor people or baby fish; Stephen Fry, the British actor and comedian, stands about six foot five.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names young fish, as in the idiom small fry, and also a very tall English performer.

clue.text: Old South Americans concealed by Joaquin Castillo

indicators.note: what is concealed is kept out of sight inside something else, here a run of printed letters

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first name and the start of the surname

explanation.surface: A man with a Spanish name hides some ancient Peruvians.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hispanic name fits the South American surface neatly, which helps disguise the join between the words.
explanation.definitionFit: The Inca people ruled an empire in the Andes before the Spanish conquest, so they are old South Americans.

clue.text: Dull working-class laddie in a Masefield story

blocks.note: dead can mean dull or lifeless, as a dead town
in Scotland a ned is a young working-class tearaway

explanation.surface: A boring lower-class boy appears in a tale by the poet laureate.
explanation.walkthrough: Ned is Scottish slang for a rough working-class youth, roughly a chav.
explanation.definitionFit: John Masefield published the novel Dead Ned in 1938, about a man hanged and revived.

clue.text: Owner of 10’s calendar

blocks.note: surface reading: the person who possesses something
setter's reading: the cross-referenced poet wrote a long rural poem whose title gives this calendar to a flock-keeper

explanation.surface: Asking who owns a particular poet's calendar.
explanation.walkthrough: 10 across is John Clare, whose 1827 poem cycle is The Shepherd's Calendar; the possessive in that title names the calendar's owner.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of Clare's poem assigns the calendar to a sheep-keeper, so the owner is that rural figure.

clue.text: Maybe Montgomery’s happy in a Buchan tale …

blocks.note: Montgomery Castle in Wales is one example of this kind of fortress
gay in its older sense of merry

explanation.surface: Field Marshal Montgomery is cheerful in a John Buchan adventure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Montgomery' suggests the general, but 'Maybe' marks an example: Montgomery is a Welsh town with a ruined castle.
explanation.definitionFit: John Buchan wrote the 1930 novel Castle Gay, one of his Galloway thrillers featuring Dickson McCunn.

clue.text: … and this poet madly turned out a form of calendar

indicators.note: to turn someone out is to evict them, so these letters are thrown out of the word
acting madly means acting wildly, so what is left is jumbled

blocks.note: the joining word of the clue, read as letters to remove
taken as written

explanation.surface: A deranged poet who produced a kind of almanac, continuing the previous clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis makes 'and' look like a link from 9 across, but it is the letters to strike from CALENDAR. 'Madly' is also apt: John Clare spent decades in asylums.
explanation.definitionFit: John Clare, the Northamptonshire peasant poet, wrote The Shepherd's Calendar, so he is the poet indicated.

clue.text: Fun play’s something to read

blocks.note: a riot is great fun, as in 'it was a riot'
to act is to play a part

explanation.surface: A comic drama turns out to be worth reading.
explanation.walkthrough: To read someone the riot act is to scold them severely; the original 1714 Act was literally read aloud to disperse crowds.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'read the riot act' makes this law something one proverbially reads out as a stern warning.

clue.text: China’s possible location, we hear, for working together

indicators.note: what we hear is a spoken version, so the spelling may differ from the sound

blocks.note: china plates and cups waiting to be washed are often in the kitchen basin

explanation.surface: Speculating where a country is sited, as heard by listeners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' looks like the country but is crockery, which sits in the sink for washing.
explanation.definitionFit: Being synchronised means acting in perfect time with others, which is cooperating or working together.

clue.text: Lying trickster’s malicious, and devious with hackery

indicators.note: devious means winding and indirect, so the letters take a crooked route

blocks.note: ill as in ill will, meaning harmful or spiteful
W is the abbreviation for with
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dishonest conman is spiteful and crafty with hack journalism.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is Australian slang, made famous by Peter Carey's 1985 novel narrated by a 139-year-old liar.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australian slang this is a confidence man or professional swindler, a lying trickster exactly.

clue.text: Lady meeting Bush, embracing together with lovers

indicators.note: to embrace is to wrap one's arms round, so one piece holds another inside

blocks.note: her is the pronoun for a lady
the oleander is a flowering evergreen shrub
and means together with

explanation.surface: A woman meets a US president who hugs her, alongside some romantic partners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bush' suggests George Bush, but it is a plant; the shrub opens after its first letter to take in the joining word.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek myth's priestess and the youth who swam the Hellespont nightly to her are a famous pair of tragic sweethearts.

clue.text: A born lawyer is also a poet

blocks.note: an is the other form of the indefinite article
né, French for born, used of a man's former name
Atticus Finch is the lawyer in To Kill a Mockingbird

explanation.surface: Someone with a natural gift for law also writes verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A born lawyer' reads as one with innate talent, but it splits into article, the French for born, and a famous fictional attorney.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne Finch, Countess of Winchilsea, was an English poet of the early eighteenth century, known for nature verse.

clue.text: A girl with a fish is one who lived by a lake

definitions.text: one who lived by a lake

blocks.note: Eva is a girl's name
the trout is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: A girl holding a fish is someone who used to live lakeside.
explanation.walkthrough: The fish and lake suggest an angler; the answer is the title heroine of Elizabeth Bowen's last novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Bowen's 1968 heroine spends her troubled youth at Larkins, a house on a lake, so she lived by water.

clue.text: The light that may allow Jessica to see her lover?

definitions.text: The light that may allow Jessica to see her lover?

blocks.note: surface reading: illumination letting someone see

blocks.clueFragment: that may allow Jessica to see her lover?
blocks.note: setter's reading: a light is a pane, and Shylock's daughter, living in the Italian lagoon city, looks down from one to Lorenzo

explanation.surface: Wondering what lamp might help a young woman glimpse her sweetheart.
explanation.walkthrough: Jessica in The Merchant of Venice elopes with Lorenzo after speaking to him from her father's casement; 'light' is an old word for a glazed opening.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a tall three-part window, arched in the middle, an architectural style named after the Italian city, matching Jessica's home.

clue.text: Joint, darling, in speech more necessary in Shakespeare

indicators.note: in speech means as spoken, so the sounds count rather than the spelling

blocks.note: the knee is a leg joint
dear is a term of affection

explanation.surface: A loving 'darling' tucked into a remark about a body part being required.
explanation.walkthrough: The modern sense is poorer, but Shakespeare used the word to mean more needful, which is why the definition is tagged.
explanation.definitionFit: In Elizabethan usage the comparative of needy could mean more urgently required, an archaic sense of 'more necessary'.

clue.text: Borneo’s exotic playwright

indicators.note: exotic means strange and foreign, so the letters appear in an unfamiliar form

blocks.note: the island's name with its possessive s

explanation.surface: A dramatist from an Asian island seems strange and foreign.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive s is part of the fodder, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: John Osborne wrote Look Back in Anger, the 1956 drama that launched the Angry Young Men.

clue.text: Sign of doubt a man has about Persephone’s driver

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: contraction of 'he has'
erm is a hesitant noise of uncertainty

explanation.surface: A man hesitates over who chauffeured the goddess of the underworld.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A man has' must be read as a contraction, he's, which then wraps the hesitation sound.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Homeric Hymn the messenger god drives Hades' chariot to bring Persephone back up to her mother Demeter.

clue.text: Comedy version of this is now Harold Pinter drama

definitions.text: Comedy version of this is now Harold Pinter drama

blocks.note: surface reading: a funny adaptation of some work
setter's reading: a West End playhouse once called the Comedy was renamed in 2011 to honour Pinter

explanation.surface: A comic rewrite of something has become a Pinter play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comedy' is a proper name, not a genre: London's Comedy Theatre in Panton Street became the Harold Pinter Theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: A playhouse building is the venue type, and the London Comedy venue now bears the dramatist's name.

clue.text: & 4: Florence possibly follows child, male, in this poem by 14

blocks.note: a tot is a small child
he is the male pronoun
Florence Nightingale, the Crimean War nurse, is one bearer of the name

explanation.surface: The Italian city perhaps comes after a boy in a verse by the cross-referenced poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Florence' looks like the Italian city but is the nurse; 'follows' puts her surname after the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne Finch, the answer at 14, wrote the ode To the Nightingale, so this is the poem referred to.

clue.text: A note on a story is kindly

blocks.note: taken as written
F is a musical note
a fable is a moral tale

explanation.surface: A comment written on a tale is gentle in tone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' looks like a written comment but is a single musical letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Affable means friendly and easy to talk to, a near synonym of kindly as an adjective.

clue.text: One’s on a long river – it could be a statement about a journey in which someone was …

definitions.text: a statement about a journey in which someone was …

blocks.note: the Ob is a long Siberian river
I is the Roman numeral one, placed on the river
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone on a great river, with a remark about a voyage in which a person was lost.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs into the next clue: someone was TAKEN FROM us. The Latin for 'he or she died' is carved on memorials, and death is the journey.
explanation.definitionFit: This Latin verb appears on tombs and in records to state that a person departed this life, the final voyage.

clue.text: … — us

blocks.note: surface reading: continuing the previous clue's sentence
setter's reading: the dash is a blank, completing the euphemism for someone who has died

explanation.walkthrough: Read 23 across straight on: 'a journey in which someone was … us'; the dash is the gap the answer fills, a gentle phrase for dying.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying a person was removed from our company is a common euphemism in obituaries and eulogies for death.

clue.text: “— is like the East he grows in, A great yellow Mandarin” (G. K. Chesterton)

definitions.text: “— is like the East he grows in, A great yellow Mandarin” (G. K. Chesterton)

blocks.clueFragment: “— is like the East he grows in, A great yellow Mandarin”
blocks.note: surface reading: a quotation with its first word missing
setter's reading: the source is Chesterton's poem Song of Right and Wrong, contrasting an Eastern drink with coffee and cocoa

explanation.walkthrough: A quotation fill-in: the gap is the drink Chesterton personifies as a Chinese official, grown in the East.
explanation.definitionFit: The beverage is grown in China and India, so the poet compares it to a Mandarin of the Orient.

clue.text: A pirate on the rampage? One who was expecting to get jewellery treacherously

definitions.text: One who was expecting to get jewellery treacherously

indicators.note: rampaging is running wild, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A buccaneer running amok, hoping to seize gems by betrayal.
explanation.walkthrough: In Roman legend she opened the citadel to the Sabines for what they wore on their left arms, meaning gold bracelets, and was crushed by their shields instead.
explanation.definitionFit: The Vestal traitor bargained for the Sabines' gold armlets, so she betrayed Rome hoping for ornaments.

clue.text: Repeats performance of last act about rogues

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
a heel is a cad or rogue

explanation.surface: A company stages its final act again, about some villains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last act' sounds theatrical, but a last is a cobbler's foot-shaped form, so the act is shoe repair.
explanation.definitionFit: A cobbler fixes footwear on a last, and renewing the backs of the soles repeats that job.
